sections.body:
Most patients believe doctors want more detail. In practice, doctors want **better-arranged** detail. The information in the room is usually enough. What is often missing is the order, the timing and the precision, and those three things are what let a clinician narrow a list of possible causes down in minutes instead of half an hour.

A symptom is something you notice and describe: pain, dizziness, a cough, a lump, sleeplessness. A **sign** is something the clinician observes for themselves: a raised temperature, a rash on examination, a heart rate of 110. You supply the symptoms, they find the signs. Both halves are needed.

Five facts carry most of the weight in any symptom report.

When it started. Not just the day, but the time of day, the day of the week, and what was happening. A pain that wakes you at 3 a.m. and settles by day is a different clue from one that appears after lunch every day.

Where it is. As precisely as you can. "In my chest" is a start; "behind the breastbone, spreading into my left jaw" is an answer. "Stomach" may mean the upper abdomen, the lower abdomen or the pain of wind, and the doctor has to guess.

How it feels. Doctors have a vocabulary for this and they use it: sharp, dull, burning, cramping, throbbing, stabbing, tight, heavy, electric. Describing a pain as "bad" tells the doctor nothing. Describing it as "burning, like hot water on skin" tells them a great deal.

How bad it is. Use a scale from zero to ten, and say what the numbers mean for you. "Seven out of ten, which stops me walking" is useful. Seven out of ten in two different people means two very different things.

What changes it. What makes it better, what makes it worse, what makes it appear. Relief and aggravation are often more diagnostic than the symptom itself.

Then two more things, which are not about the symptom but about you: the **medicines you take** and the **conditions you have had before**. Many consultations turn on a medicine the patient did not mention because it was bought years ago and used occasionally.

That is the whole structure. If you can give those seven things clearly, you have given a doctor more usable information than most patients give in ten minutes of unstructured talking.
examples: It started four days ago, in the evening, and it has been there every evening since.
It is a dull ache behind the breastbone, about six out of ten, worse when I lie flat.
The pain is on the right side, not the left, and it is worse after I eat.
sections.heading: What a doctor actually needs from you

sections.body:
The instinct is to describe the sensation first, because that is what frightens you. Clinicians often want the opposite. **Timing** is the frame the symptom sits in, and it narrows the possibilities faster than any description of the sensation.

Four timing facts are worth having ready.

Onset. How it began: suddenly, like a switch, or gradually, creeping in over days. Sudden onset suggests something acute, such as a blockage, a bleed or an infection. Gradual onset suggests something cumulative, such as a strain, a wear-and-tear change or a slow illness. This distinction alone changes which investigations are sensible.

Pattern. Is it constant, or does it come and go? If it comes and goes, how long does each episode last? Is it the same every time, or does it vary? A symptom that lasts five minutes and a symptom that lasts five hours are not the same symptom.

Course. Since it began, has it stayed the same, got steadily worse, or come and gone? Improvement is a fact too, and it is often the most useful fact of all.

Trigger. What was happening in the hours before it started: a meal, exercise, a particular position, an argument, a long drive, a night of poor sleep, a new medicine. Often you will not know. Saying "I cannot tell what triggered it" is a perfectly good answer.

Write the timing down as a short line before you go, because it is the part that evaporates under pressure. Something like: *started Tuesday evening, after a long walk; worse at night, better after sitting up; roughly one hour at a time, twice a day; no clear trigger*.

One caution. Do not turn your description into a diagnosis. Saying "it is probably my heart" moves the consultation away from the description and towards reassuring you, which is not what you are there for. Say what you feel, when you feel it and how much it limits you, and let the clinician do the naming.
examples: It came on suddenly in the middle of the night, and it woke me up.
Each episode lasts about ten minutes, and it happens once or twice a day.
It has been getting worse over the last two weeks.
It usually starts after I have eaten, maybe half an hour later.
sections.heading: Start with when, not what

sections.body:
Three questions come up at almost every consultation: **where**, **what does it feel like**, and **how bad**. They are worth answering with the same structure every time, because a consistent answer is easy to compare and a vague one has to be re-asked.

Where. Point to it on your own body if you can, and say which side. Left and right are the most useful words in the whole consultation, because the body is not symmetrical and clinicians think in sides. Then say whether the pain stays where it started or travels, and if it travels, in which direction. Pain that starts in the lower back and travels down the back of one leg to the ankle is a completely different report from pain that stays in the lower back.

What it feels like. Borrow the words doctors use, because they are precise rather than dramatic. Sharp and cutting. Dull and aching. Burning, as if hot water had been poured. Cramping, in waves that come and go. Throbbing, in time with the heartbeat. Tight, as if something were squeezing. Stabbing, sudden and short. Heaviness, as if something were sitting on it. Electric, shooting along a line. If a word does not fit, say so. "It is not burning, more like a heavy ache" is a good answer.

How bad. Give a number from zero to ten, and then anchor it. Zero is no pain at all, ten is the worst pain you can imagine. Then say what the number stops you doing, because that is what matters. Six out of ten, and I cannot sit down for longer than ten minutes. Three out of ten, and it is in the background but I can work.

Two habits make this much stronger. First, describe what it does **not** affect, because the doctor may be checking for that. "It does not affect my breathing, and I have not been sick" is often as informative as the symptom itself.

Second, if the symptom comes and goes, describe it at its worst rather than at its average. Doctors have to plan around the worst case, and the average case hides the pattern that matters.
examples: It is on the left side, and it travels down to my wrist.
It is a burning pain, and it is worse at night than during the day.
It is about seven out of ten, and I cannot drive with it.
It does not affect my breathing, and I have not felt sick at all.
sections.heading: Where it is, how it feels, and how bad

sections.body:
This part of the history is called **relieving and aggravating factors**, and it is often the most decisive thing you can offer. It is also the part patients forget, because they only think of the symptom itself.

The categories are simple. **Position**: does it change when you lie down, sit up, bend, turn your neck? **Movement**: does it change when you walk, stretch, lift? **Food and drink**: does eating help, hurt, or trigger it? **Time of day**: is it worse in the morning or at night? **Stress**: does a busy week make it worse? **Heat and cold**: does a hot shower relax it? **Medication**: does a painkiller help, and for how long? **Bodily functions**: does anything you do change it, such as coughing, sneezing, moving your bowels or passing urine?

The last category is easy to miss and often the most valuable. A pain that gets worse when you cough or sneeze points towards something structural. A symptom that changes with urination points somewhere else entirely. A headache that is different when you lie down is a different headache from one that is not.

The answer that helps most is quantitative. "It is better after I walk, but if I walk more than ten minutes it comes back" is a much better answer than "walking helps". You are describing the shape of the symptom, and shape is what the clinician uses to fit it to a cause.

Watch the difference between relief and cause. If a pain eases when you take paracetamol, that does not mean paracetamol caused it. Say "paracetamol takes the edge off for about two hours", not "paracetamol causes it".

And one more question worth asking yourself, because you may know it and not think it matters: has anything changed recently? A new job with long hours, a new medication, a new diet, a new pillow, a new running shoes, a pregnancy, a bereavement, a move to a new house. Doctors are trained to ask about this, and patients are often the only ones who can spot the connection.
examples: It is better when I sit up and worse when I lie flat.
Coughing makes it much worse, and I have to stop talking.
It eases for about an hour after I take a painkiller.
It started about a month after I changed jobs.
sections.heading: What makes it better or worse

sections.body:
Every consultation runs through the same core questions. You can prepare for all of them, and preparing makes the appointment shorter and more useful.

What brings you in today? One sentence naming the main complaint. Do not list five things. Say the one that brought you here, and mention the others when asked.

How long has it been going on? Have the answer ready. "Three weeks" is enough if you are unsure.

Is it there all the time? Or only sometimes?

Does anything make it better or worse?

Have you noticed anything else? Reviewing the body system by system. Most clinicians will sweep through this: your head and neck, your chest, your heart, your stomach and digestion, your kidneys and urine, your joints and muscles, your skin, your nerves, and your sleep and mood. A symptom that seems unrelated to the main complaint may belong to this list, so it is worth having thought about it.

What have you tried so far? Include over-the-counter medicines, home remedies, herbal products and anything a neighbour recommended. Everything you took matters, even if it did not work.

What medicines do you take? Name them all, including the ones you take only occasionally and the ones for conditions you no longer have. Doses and timings help too.

Do you have any allergies? Reactions to medicines, foods, latex, and what happened.

Any medical problems in the past? Hospital stays, operations, chronic conditions, mental health, and anything serious in the family.

What do you do for a living, and who lives with you? Occupation, exposures, and sometimes who prepares your food. It surprises people, but it is asked for a reason.

What do you think is happening? You will be asked this, and you are entitled to answer honestly. Say what worries you and why. Clinicians often have the same worry, and naming it lets them address it directly instead of guessing.
examples: The main problem is the pain in my right shoulder, which has been there three weeks.
I have been taking ibuprofen twice a day for the last four days.
I am allergic to penicillin; I get a rash and I swell around the mouth.
I am worried it is something serious, because my father had something similar.
sections.heading: The questions you will be asked, and how to answer them

sections.body:
You will hear these words, and it helps to know what they are asking for so that you answer the right thing.

Symptom is something you feel and report. **Sign** is something the clinician finds by examining you. **History** is the story of the problem up to today. **Prodrome** is the vague set of early symptoms that come before a condition fully appears, such as the tiredness and sore throat that precede a cold.

Acute means coming on quickly and lasting a short time. **Chronic** means long-standing, usually over three months. **Exacerbation** is a period when symptoms get worse; **remission** is a period when they settle or disappear.

Intermittent means coming and going. **Constant** means present all the time. **Unilateral** means on one side; **bilateral** means on both. **Radiating** means spreading along a line, usually of nerve or muscle.

Idiopathic means the cause is not known. When a clinician says "idiopathic", it means they can see the effect clearly and cannot name the mechanism, which is a statement about knowledge rather than about you.

Differential diagnosis is the clinician's shortlist of possible causes. When they say "the differential includes three things", they are telling you what they are excluding, and you are entitled to ask what each one is.

Investigation is any test: blood tests, imaging, a scan, a sample. **Referral** is a letter sending you to another service, such as a specialist or a physiotherapist.

Side effect and **symptom** are different animals. A side effect comes from the medicine; a symptom comes from your body. Keep the two separate in your notes, because conflating them is a common reason for a problem going unrecognised.
sections.heading: The words doctors use, and how to answer them

terms.example: The main symptom is the pain, and it has been there for three weeks.
terms.gloss: Something you notice and describe yourself: pain, dizziness, a cough, a lump.

terms.example: My temperature was high, and the doctor found a rash on my legs.
terms.gloss: Something the clinician finds by examining you, such as a fever or a rash, rather than something you report.

terms.example: This is an acute episode, and it started yesterday.
terms.gloss: Coming on quickly and lasting a short time, usually days.

terms.example: It has become a chronic problem, so I have started to manage it differently.
terms.gloss: Long-standing, generally present for more than three months.

terms.example: The main exacerbation lasted about four days last month.
terms.gloss: A period when the symptoms get noticeably worse than their usual level.

terms.example: The doctor said the differential included three possibilities, and explained each one.
terms.gloss: The clinician's shortlist of possible causes, kept in mind while they examine you and order tests.

terms.example: I have a referral for a scan, and the appointment is in ten days.
terms.gloss: A letter sending you to another service, such as a specialist, a physiotherapist or a scan.

sections.body:
Some symptoms must not wait for a routine appointment, and some must not wait for a phone call. Seek emergency care immediately for chest pain or pressure, pain that spreads into the arm, jaw or back, sudden severe breathlessness, a face or arm that droops or is suddenly weak, sudden confusion or difficulty speaking, a seizure, a severe allergic reaction with swelling or trouble breathing, heavy bleeding that will not stop, a severe burn, a suspected broken neck or back after an accident, or any sudden severe headache unlike your usual ones.

The same day, not the next appointment, is right for a fever with a stiff neck or a rash that does not fade under pressure, vomiting that will not stop and cannot keep fluids down, blood in your urine or vomit, a painful swollen calf, a wound that will not close or is spreading red and hot, a sudden severe abdominal pain, or a fall in an older person, even when the person says they feel fine. If you are unsure whether a symptom is one of these, describe it to a clinician rather than deciding on your own.
sections.heading: Red flags: when a symptom should not wait

sections.body:
Ten minutes of preparation before you leave the house makes the appointment better for both of you. The memory that feels vivid in the waiting room is often wrong about order, and it is nearly always wrong about frequency.

Write the timeline down. A short list of dated entries: when it started, when it changed, what you did about it. Even four bullet points will beat trying to remember in the room.

Make a list of everything you take. All medicines, including bought ones, herbal preparations and vitamins. Include doses. Put it in your phone or on paper, and take it with you.

Decide what your main complaint is. If you have five things wrong, the appointment will deal with the one you name first. Rank them, and ask about the rest separately.

Bring the evidence. A photo of a rash, a photo of the swelling, the packaging of the medicine, a food diary, a sleep log, a temperature reading, or a video of a movement that worries you. A ten-second video often tells a clinician more than a paragraph of description.

Ask someone to come with you if the consultation is important or complex. A second pair of ears catches half of what you are told, and you are allowed to ask the clinician to slow down and explain. You may also record the consultation on your phone, after asking permission. Many clinics allow it, and it removes the problem of forgetting half the instructions on the walk home.

Bring your questions written down. You will not remember them in the room. Ask them at the end, and ask about what happens next: what will be monitored, when should you come back, and what should make you contact the surgery sooner.
examples: I have written the timeline down, with the dates.
Here is a photo of the rash from yesterday morning.
Can I record this on my phone so I remember what you said?
sections.heading: Preparing: notes, a list, and a witness

sections.body: Run this routine before every appointment that matters. It takes ten minutes and it changes the consultation.
examples: My main problem is the burning in my stomach when I eat.
I have written my questions so I do not forget them.
sections.heading: Ten minutes of preparation before the consultation
steps: Write one sentence naming your main problem.
Write the timeline: when it started, how it has changed.
Write down where it is, what it feels like, and how bad it is out of ten.
Write what makes it better and what makes it worse.
List every medicine, supplement and remedy you take, with doses.
Collect evidence: photos, videos, temperature readings, packaging.
Write your questions, and put them somewhere you will find them.
Bring someone with you if the appointment is complex or emotional.

sections.body:
The consultation is not the end of the process. What happens in the next hour decides whether the next month goes well.

Write down the plan before you leave. You can do it in the car park. What was the assessment, what was prescribed or requested, what were you told to watch for, and when is the next contact. If the clinician used a word you did not know, write it down and look it up. If you were given a medicine, write the exact name, the dose and how often to take it.

Do not leave with an unclear instruction. If you do not know whether to take a medicine before food or after, or whether you need a blood test first, ask before you stand up. The commonest source of wasted appointments and doubled doses is a fuzzy instruction at the end of a rushed consultation.

Ask what would make it worse. Every plan has a trigger. "If the pain gets worse, or you get a fever, or you develop numbness, contact us" is the most useful sentence in the whole visit. Knowing it in advance means you act early rather than waiting for it to be unbearable.

Keep a symptom diary if the plan involves watching. Dates, triggers, severity out of ten, and what you took. After two weeks, this diary is often more informative than the symptom itself, and it is the basis for any decision to change treatment.

Do not stop a medicine early because you feel better. Feeling better is the treatment working, not the treatment being unnecessary. If you want to stop, ask, and ask how to reduce it if it must be tapered.

Go back sooner than you think you should. If the plan was to wait and see, and the symptom changes in a way that worries you, contact the surgery. Nobody has ever been criticised for a phone call that turned out to be unnecessary. The cost of a wasted call is a minute; the cost of a waited-on symptom can be months.
examples: The plan is: this medicine for five days, and I call back if it has not helped by Friday.
You said it might be the muscle, but if I get numbness or the pain spreads, what should I do?
I have started a diary: date, what I did, the pain out of ten, and what I took.
I feel better, but I will keep taking it until you tell me to stop.
sections.heading: After the appointment: what to write down and what to do

item.summary: Doctors do not need more detail, they need better-arranged detail. After reading this you can describe a symptom so precisely that the doctor can narrow the cause quickly, answer the standard questions in full, and know when a symptom needs urgent care instead of a routine appointment.
item.title: How to Describe Symptoms to a Doctor
